Bio-pretreatment promote hydrolysis and acidification of oilseed rape straw:
Roles of fermentation broth and micro-oxygen
Chuqiao Wanga,1, Jiajie Zhanga,1, Fengping Hua, Shuai Zhangb,⁎, Ji Luc, Shuai Liud
a School of Civil Engineering and Architecture, East China Jiaotong University, Nanchang 330013, China
b Jiangsu Key Laboratory of Atmospheric Environment Monitoring and Pollution Control (AEMPC), Collaborative Innovation Center of Atmospheric Environment and
Equipment Technology (CIC-AEET), Nanjing University of Information Science & Technology, Nanjing 210044, China
c Advanced Water Management Centre (AWMC), The University of Queensland, St Lucia, Brisbane, QLD 4072, Australia
d College of Environment and Safety Engineering, Qingdao University of Science and Technology, Qingdao, Shandong Province 266042, China
G R A P H I C A L A B S T R A C T
A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords:
Bio-pretreatment
Oilseed rape straw
Micro-oxygen
Hydrolysis
Acidification
A B S T R A C T
Oilseed rape straw (ORS) is capable of producing renewable energy. However, cellulose, hemicellulose and
lignin are intertwined together in ORS, which makes it difficult for anaerobic digestion (AD). Hence, pretreat-
ment is the key factor in reducing the rate-limiting step of AD. This study reports that the pretreatment combined
fermentation broth and micro-oxygen could enhance the degradation of ORS. The maximum biodegradation
ratios of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin (CHL) were 20.6%, 18.1%, and 24.7%, respectively, at 120 mL/
gVS/d oxygen load. The maximum volatile fatty acids and soluble chemical oxygen demand of hydrolysis and
acidification of the pretreated groups were significantly higher than that of the control groups. Microorganisms
in the fermentation broth at micro-aerobic conditions led to the reduction of CHL content, and altered the
structure of ORS. The fermentation broth bio-pretreatment could effectively decrease the functional groups
related to lignin.
1. Introduction
In China, oilseed rape straw (ORS) (kind of dicotyledonous crop) is
one of the widely cultivated oil-crops. More than 20 million tons of ORS
are produced each year (Wang et al., 2017a,b). The ORS has been re-
cognized as a source of renewable energy. Anaerobic digestion (AD) is
known as a widely used and cost-effective way to convert agriculture
biomass into biogas (Sawatdeenarunat et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2019).

However, cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin are intertwined with each
other and forming complex structures in ORS, which makes it difficult
to be decomposed by the microorganisms during the AD process
(Patinvoh et al., 2017).
It is recognized that the rate-limiting step of AD mediates the initial
hydrolysis process of macromolecular organic matter or non-degraded
organics, especially in the two-stage anaerobic digestion. Hence, pre-
treatment of the straw before hydrolysis has been considered as an
essential step (Tian et al., 2012). Thus, several efforts have been made
to enhance the efficiency of AD, such as thermal pretreatment (Luo
et al., 2019; Phuttaro et al., 2019), thermal-chemical pretreatment
mechanical pretreatment (Qiao et al., 2018; Vivekanand et al., 2012),
and biological pretreatment (Guan et al., 2018; Guo et al., 2019). In
addition, steam explosion has been reported as an effective method that
resulted in the transformation of hemicellulose under explosive de-
compression (Wood et al., 2014). The alkali pretreatment is also an
effective and commonly used way to selectively remove lignin from
lignocelluloses (Sun et al., 2015). However, the extra energy or che-
micals are often required in these physicochemical treatment methods,
which leads to the increased cost and difficulties in recovering the
chemicals. Thus, these physic-chemical pretreatments have rarely been
applied in a full-scale plant (Carrere et al., 2016). Compared with
physical and chemical pretreatment methods, biological pretreatment is
a relatively inexpensive and low energy demand upstream technology.
Up to now, extensive studies have been done on biological pre-
treatment of lignocellulose, such as enzymatic, fungi, composting and
ensiling pretreatments (Xu et al., 2018). However, it might be difficult
to widely application in biogas plants due to the cost of microbial
strains and enzymes (Carrere et al., 2016). In addition, N element was
added to adjust the C/N ratio in white-rot fungi biological pretreatment
inoculants (Castoldi et al., 2014). In the actual biogas production pro-
cess, a large amount of biogas slurry and biogas residue would be
produced. More importantly, the biogas slurry usually contained a high
concentration of ammonia nitrogen that can cause water pollution
(Chen et al., 2017). However, the treatment of ammonia nitrogen in
biogas slurry focuses on the recovery of additional chemicals, which
results in a relatively high cost. The pretreatment of the straw with the
fermentation broth containing microorganisms can be a promising
pretreatment inoculum, and the nitrogen element (NH4
+- N) can be
used as nutrition for the microorganism grow (Guo et al., 2019).
A previous study found that aerobic pretreatment could lead to low
volatile fatty acids (VFAs) concentration and high alkalinity. However,
methane production from per unit of volatile solids (VS) was not im-
proved (Ward et al., 1998). In addition, the micro-aerobic condition in
anaerobic digester by the addition of a low oxygen dose could sig-
nificantly increase the hydrolysis rate of lignocellulosic (Fu et al., 2016)
and methane production in the anaerobic process (Ramos and Fdz-
Polanco, 2013; Xu et al., 2018). Up to now, it is unclear whether ORS
could promote the AD ability with fermentation broth under micro-
aerobic condition. The objective of this study is to investigate the effects
of the bio-pretreatment on VFAs production and several anaerobic
fermentation parameters.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Raw materials
The ORS used in this study was collected from Hexian District,
Maanshan City, Anhui Province, China. The ORS was laid over the field
and dry under the sun for 1 week, and the moisture content was about
10%. The contents of C and N in ORS were 44.51 ± 0.32% and
0.88 ± 0.11%, respectively, TS and VS were 91.21 ± 0.66% and
86.63 ± 0.53%, respectively. The cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin
contents were 40.64 ± 0.92%, 23.15 ± 0.87% and 21.33 ± 0.54%,
respectively. The pretreatment liquid used for the pretreatment was
taken from the hydrolysis acidification reactor of the two-phase anae-
robic reactor, which was normally operated in the laboratory. The
substrate was a mixture of rapeseed straw, kitchen waste and duck feces
with a dry matter ratio of 2:1:1 (Wang et al., 2017a,b). The pH of the
pretreatment liquid was 6.81 ± 0.16. sCOD concentration, VFAs
concentration
and
ammonia

were
0.78 ± 0.11 g/L, 0.45 ± 0.08 g/L and 3.2 ± 0.18 g/L, respectively.
The microbial community structure analysis of pretreatment liquid
showed that there were a total of 16 identified bacterial phyla and a
total of 7 identified fungal class. The most dominant bacterial phyla was
Bacteroidetes (50.26%), and followed by Firmicutes (15.37%) and Pro-
teobacteria (9.34%). The most dominant fungal class was Sordar-
iomycetes (44.99%), and followed by Dothideomycetes (25.56%) and
Eurotiomycetes (17.9%).
2.2. Biological micro-aerobic pretreatment
Micro-aerobic pretreatment was applied to treat the ORS upstream
phased anaerobic digestion. Before pretreatment, the 500 mL wide-
mouth jars were autoclaved for 20 min at 121 °C. Every 30 g of straw
was placed in a 500 mL wide-mouth jar, evenly sprayed with 58 mL of
fermentation broth from phased anaerobic digester (hydrolysis acid-
ification reactor) and evenly stirred with Titanium stick. The pretreat-
ment moisture content was 65%, and the pretreatment time was 10 d.
The jars were sealed with perforated rubber stoppers. Micro air pumps
(1 L/min) were used to ventilate the aeration head installed in the
middle of the bottle bottom. The oxygen loads were 0, 20, 60 and
120 mL/gVS/d, corresponding to T0, T1, T2 and T3 test. The ORS in the
control group used deionized water instead of fermentation broth.
In order to investigate the role of microorganisms and other com-
ponents (eg. organic acids), the hydrolysis acidification liquid was
treated as follows: in T4 test, the liquid was filtered through 0.22 μm
microporous membrane (33 mm/0.22 µm, Millipore, USA) and used as
a sterilization pretreatment liquid. The oxygen load of T4 was 20 mL/
gVS/d (optimal oxygen load in previous laboratory experiments).
After the pretreatment, the solid residue was filtered and washed
several times by deionized water until neutral. The collected dry solids
were used for hydrolysis and acidification tests and other analyses. The
experiments were carried out in triplicates for each group. At the end of
the pre-treatment, the straw samples were taken out to determine CHL
(cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin) content and dry weight. The de-
gradation ratio of CHL of pretreated ORS was calculated as Eq. (1).

2.3. Hydrolysis and acidification test
Pretreated ORS or untreated ORS were mixed with inoculum (taken
from laboratory hydrolysis acidification reactor) in a 250 mL serum
bottles. The working volume and the total TS loading were controlled at
200 mL and 60 g TS/L, respectively.
All serum bottles were tightly closed with butyl rubber stoppers and
aluminum-plastics combined caps. No additional nutrient solution was
added to anaerobic hydrolysis and acidification tests. All the serum
bottles were placed in constant temperature shaker incubator (Xinrui,
THZ-82, China) at 35 °C and shaken 8 times per day at 100 r/min for
5 min. The hydrolytic acidification solution was sampled daily to de-
termine the sCOD and VFAs, and the remaining liquid after the analysis
was returned to the reactor with a syringe (Mohan and Bindhu, 2008).
In order to eliminate the influence of VFAs in the inoculum on the
concentration of sCOD and VFAs during hydrolysis and acidification,
the amount of sCOD and VFAs brought into the inoculum was sub-
tracted when calculating the concentration.
2.4. Analytical methods
All experiments were performed in duplicate. The analyses of total
solids (TS), volatile solids (VS) were conducted in accordance with
Standard Methods (APHA, 1998). Cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin
content were determined according to the method described by Van
Soest (Van Soest et al., 1991). sCOD and VFAs in liquid samples were
analyzed after particulate removal by centrifuged at 10,000 rpm for
10 min and filtered through 0.45 µm membrane (33 mm/0.45 µm,
Millipore, USA). The concentration of VFAs in hydrolytic acidification
fluid was measured by GC (GC-2001, Shimadzu, Japan) equipped with
hydrogen flame ionization detector (FID), using quartz capillary
column (30 m × 0.32 mm × D × 0.25 µm; Stabilwax-DA, RESTEK,
USA) with nitrogen as a carrier gas. GC operating conditions were as
follows: injector temperature at 220 °C, detector temperature at 230 °C.
Column heating procedures were as follows: the starting temperature
was maintained at 100 °C for 1 min, then at 10 °C/min rate increased to
140 °C and maintained 2 min, at last increased to 200 °C at 15 °C/min
rate and maintained 2 min.
2.5. Data analyses and statistics
The measurements were expressed as means ± standard deviation.
The significant differences between groups were determined using one-
way analysis of variance. The significant level (p value) was set at 0.05
and 0.01. Pair-wise comparisons were conducted on sCOD concentra-
tion, VFAs concentration and the CHL degradation ratio to identify
significant differences between different groups. The Pearson correla-
tion analysis was used to analyze the correlation between experimental
data. The SPSS19.0 (IBM, USA) and OriginPro 8.5 (OriginLab, USA)
were used for data processing and graphing.
2.6. Chemical and physical analysis
In order to intuitively explore the changes of surface morphology
and internal structure of rapeseed straw under micro-aerobic pretreat-
ment, field emission scanning electron microscope (FESEM, Ultra Plus,
Zeiss, Germany) was used to analyze the untreated straw and pretreated
straw samples. The specific steps were as fellow: taking an appropriate
amount of untreated or pretreated straw granules first and then vacuum
drying with a freeze dryer (FD-1A-80, Tianling, China). The dried
samples were fixed on the silicon wafer and placed in the sample
chamber for observation at 1.0 kV.
Fourier
transform
infrared
spectroscopy
(FTIR,
Nicolet
iS50,
Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA) was used to investigate organic func-
tional groups and structural changes in ORS. The specific steps were as
fellow: (1) weighed 1 mg of the ORS sample after freeze-drying, (2)
added 100 mg of dried potassium bromide powder, (3) mixed well, (4)
ground in an agate mortar and putted into a molding machine, (5)
vacuumed to increase pressure and made into a transparent tablet
under pressure. The pellets were placed in a Fourier transform infrared
spectrometer (iS50, Thermo Scientific Nicolet, USA) with a resolution
of 4 cm−1 and a number of scans of 30.
X-ray diffraction (XRD, SmartLab3, Rigaku, Japan) was used to in-
vestigate crystalline structure changes in ORS, and use diffraction in-
tensity to calculate the crystallinity index of cellulose (Zhao et al.,
2016a,b). The specific steps were as fellow: grinded the ORS sample
with agate mortar after freeze-drying, and putted the sifted ORS sample
in X-ray diffractometer (Smartlab (3), Rigaku Corporation, Japan) for
measurement. XRD operating conditions were as follows: Cu target, Ni
filter, tube current was 30 mA, tube voltage was 40 KV, scan mode was
2θ/θ scan, the measuring range of angle was 10–60°, scan rate was 5°/
min.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Micro-oxygen increase bio-pretreatment of ORS
To measure the effects of fermentation broth and micro-oxygen on
the degradation of ORS, the biodegradation rates of cellulose, hemi-
cellulose, and lignin were evaluated. Cellulose and hemicellulose in
ORS are the main carbon sources during the anaerobic process (Zhong
et al., 2011). Changes in cellulose, hemicellulose, lignin, TS and VS of
ORS after the pretreatment process were shown in Table 1. After the
pretreatment, both TS and VS were reduced with the increase of oxygen
load. The lignin and cellulose content were reduced with the oxygen
load increased, and the content of hemicellulose were remained stable.
Though decreasing lignin content could improve the biological acces-
sibility of treated ORS, the cellulose content was also dropped down.
Oxygen supply is one of the particularly important factors for the
ORS pretreatment. However, excess oxygen would lead to the massive
proliferation of aerobic microorganisms, which result in the easily de-
gradable COD directly oxidized to H2O and CO2 during micro-aerobic
pretreatment (Zitomer and Shrout, 1998). The degradation ratios of

lignin, hemicellulose and cellulose of ORS under micro-aerobic bio-
pretreatments were shown in Fig. 1.
As shown in Fig. 1, the degradation ratio of CHL increased with the
increase of oxygen load, and the degradation of lignin was most sig-
nificant. When the oxygen load was 120 mL/gVS/d, the degradation
ratio of lignin reached 24.74% after 10 days, and the highest de-
gradation ratios of cellulose and hemicellulose were 20.61% and
18.05%, respectively. This was due to the fact that most of the hemi-
cellulose and cellulose in the straw were encapsulated by lignin, and the
degradation of lignin during pretreatment could increase the chances of
hemicellulose and cellulose in the interior being in contact with mi-
croorganisms (Zhao et al., 2016a,b). Most of the actinomycetes and
molds capable of degrading lignin were obligate aerobic bacteria,
which used molecular oxygen as the final electron (hydrogen) receptor
in the respiratory process. These microorganisms will be more active
and consumed more organics with the increasing oxygen load (Díaz
et al., 2011).
It's worth noting that the degradation ratio of cellulose, hemi-
cellulose and lignin were 21.02%, 18.58% and 25.03%, respectively,
when oxygen load increased to 150 mL/gVS/d. The degradation ratio of
CHL were not significantly higher (p > 0.05) than that in T3 group.
This indicates that the biodegradability of bio-pretreatment is hard to
increase further when oxygen load higher than 120 mL/gVS/d. The
CHL degradation in different pretreatments of some agro-industrial
wastes were summarized in Table 2. This study showed higher cellulose
and lignin degradation than that of traditional pretreatment (Zhou
et al., 2012). The lignin and hemicellulose degradation of ORS in this
study were similar to those of fungal pretreatment. However, fungal
pretreatment has better selectivity in lignin removal, and the cellulose
degradation in this study was higher than that of fungal pretreatment
(Ge et al., 2015). The degradation profile of ORS was also similar to rice
straw pretreated by combined biological and chemical pretreatment,
and the chemicals greatly reduce the treating time than bio-pretreat-
ment (Guan et al., 2018).
3.2. Pretreatment liquid enhances the degradation of ORS
The pretreatment liquid (fermentation broth) could increase the
degradation performance of TS, VS and CHL (Fig. 2A). For instance, the
degradation ratios of TS and VS for the ORS in the original inoculum
group were 7.27% and 7.59%, respectively. In addition, the degrada-
tion ratios of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin were 10.71%, 13.90%,
and 16.50%, respectively. These degradation ratios of VS, TS and CHL
in the T1 group (pretreatment liquid group) were significantly higher
(p < 0.05) than that of the control group (deionized water). The de-
gradation ratio of the control group showed that the loss of VS, TS and
CHL were all lower than 0.5%. This indicated that the waxy surfaces
and lignocellulose structure of ORS could prevent organic matter dis-
solved into water.

degradation ratios of straw might due to the combined effect of mi-
croorganisms and other components (organic acids) (Amnuaycheewa

3.3. Performance of hydrolysis and acidification for the bio-pretreatment
ORS
Previous research found that the sCOD was positively correlated
with methane yields during AD (Shen et al., 2014). The hydrolytic-
acidification experiment was investigated to explore the performance of
hydrolysis and acidification in the bio-pretreated ORS.
The trend of sCOD and VFAs were analyzed during the operation
period. For example, the sCOD of each group continued to rise in the
first 4 days, and tended to be gentle, reached 3789.0–6192.6 mg/L on
the 5th day, and then decreased slightly on the 6th day. While the VFAs
continued to rise to 3025.3–4667.3 mg/L in the first 5 days, and de-
creased slightly from the 6th day. This indicated that under the hy-
drolysis of microorganisms in the first 4 days, cellulose, hemicellulose
and other components in the ORS were hydrolyzed into soluble sub-
stances, and then the soluble substances were converted into volatile

Combined with the trend of VFAs and sCOD, the hydrolysis acidifica-
tion peaked on the fifth day, after which the VFAs began to be con-

treatment ORS was higher than that in the control group (without bio-
pretreated ORS). For instance, the highest VFAs concentrations in the
pretreatment group with oxygen loads of 0, 20, 60 and 120 mL/gVS/d
were 21.2%, 54.3%, 31.1% and 27.1% higher than the untreated group,
respectively. The highest concentrations of VFAs and sCOD were both

3.4. Characteristics of bio-pretreated ORS
3.4.1. Apparent morphology of ORS
As shown in the image during pretreatment, white hyphae gradually
covered the surface of the straw particles with the micro-aerobic pre-
treatment process, and the mycelium was uniformly distributed on the
surface of the straw particles at 10 days. After 25 days, the mycelium
grew into a bud. The photographs by optical microscope before and
after pretreatment shows the fiber bundles inside the untreated straw
were clearly visible, and the fibers are arranged closely and regularly.
From the optical micrograph of the pretreated straw, it can be seen that
there were obvious hyphae in the straw. These hyphae extending into
the interior could play a certain destructive effect on the initially ar-
ranged fiber tube so that more cellulose and hemicellulose could be
exposed, and the treated ORS became more accessible to hydrolytic/
acidification microorganism.
It can be seen from FESEM images that the surface structure of the
straw was tight and regular without the pretreatment of hydrolytic
acidification fluid and micro-aerobic, and there was almost no gap
between the fiber bundles. However, after the pretreatment, the surface
structure of the straw changed significantly. A large number of holes
were formed on the surface of the treated straw, and the structure be-
came disordered. The individual fiber bundles produced a spring-like
spiral structure under the microbial erosion. FESEM images shown that
microorganisms played an important role in the microaerobic pre-
treatment process. A large number of microorganisms were distributed
on the surface and inside of the straw samples. According to the mor-
phology, there were bacteria, actinomycetes and fungi. These micro-
organisms could

3.4.2. FTIR analysis
The components in the ORS are composed of some basic structural
units and these units have specific chemical groups. Therefore, changes
in the composition of ORS before and after pretreatment were analyzed
by FTIR. As shown in infrared spectra, the symmetrical or anti-sym-
metric stretching vibration of –CH3, –CH2 and aliphatic CH near 2920/
cm was weakened after the micro-aerobic biological pretreatment. It
can be speculated that this was related to the breakage of some fatty
chains in oilseed rape straw and the degradation of some carbohy-
drates. After pretreatment, the C]O stretching vibration associated
with the aromatic ring near 1636–1634/cm was significantly wea-
kened, which indicated that the lignin in the straw was degraded. The
absorption peaks around 1509, 1424, and 1326/cm were also related to
lignin, which was related to the benzene ring, the methyl group C–H,
and the lilac ring. The three absorption peaks decreased slightly after
pretreatment, which was consistent with the lignin degradation in the
ORS as shown in Fig. 1.
The peak intensity of the straw after pretreatment at 1245/cm was
much weaker than that of the untreated straw, which was related to the
microbial degradation of the guaiac aromatic ring in the pretreatment
process (Zhao et al., 2016a,b). The absorption peak near 1066/cm was
related to the vibration of the C-O extension peak of cellulose and
hemicellulose, and was also related to the stretching vibration of siloxy
group in silica (O-Si-O) (Zhao et al., 2016a,b). The spectra showed that
the spikes near 1066/cm were wider and more gradual after pretreat-
ment, which indicated that the crystalline silicon and cellulose in the
rape straw had been transformed (Fu et al., 2015a,b). When wheat
straw was treated with NaOH, the absorption peak near 1066 dis-
appeared, mainly because NaOH can break the ester bond between
carbohydrate and lignin, thereby released the fibers wrapped in lignin
(Fu et al., 2015a,b).
3.4.3. XRD analysis
In the aspect of straw against biodegradation, the crystalline cellu-
lose is harder accessible to cellulase attack than amorphous cellulose
has been widely accepted. It means biodegradation of ORS is inverse to
the amount of crystalline cellulose. Therefore, changes in crystallinity
of ORS before and after pretreatment were analyzed by XRD. After
biological micro-aerobic pretreatment, the main broad peak at 22° and
peak at 16.2°, which corresponding to the crystalline portion and the
amorphous portion of ORS (Dhabhai et al., 2013). The calculated
crystallinity indexes of untreated and pretreated ORS were 39.25% and
35.11%, respectively. This indicates that biological micro-aerobic pre-
treatment modified the crystallographic structure of rape straw, and
reduced the amount of crystalline cellulose present in the rape straw.
Hence the improvement of hydrolysis and acidification efficiency of
ORS can be attributed to the crystalline cellulose reduced in the pre-
treatment process.
4. Conclusions
This study proved that fermentation broth could enhance the bio-
degradation of ORS under micro-aerobic conditions. Results showed
that CHL degradation of ORS can be increased with oxygen load in-
creased from 0 to 120 mL/gVS/d. The maximum concentrations of
VFAs and sCOD were obtained at 20 mL/gVS/d oxygen load.
Microorganisms in fermentation broth played critical roles during the
pretreatment process. The physical and chemical characterizations of
bio-pretreated ORS showed that the destruction of functional groups
related to lignin and reduction of cellulose crystallinity index might be
the reason for the improvement of hydrolysis and acidification.
